title: Why NASA Brought Two Satellites Back to Earth
subtitle: Two stranded satellites. Five astronauts. A second chance at orbit.
description: The true story of Discovery's STS-51A satellite recovery mission in 1984.

publication.description: In 1984, two communications satellites reached space and ended up in the wrong orbits. Their hardware still worked. Their businesses could not. Months later, five astronauts aboard Discovery set out to bring them home. The mission joined the ambitions of the space shuttle program with an unusual insurance recovery, then confronted the crew with a problem their capture equipment could not solve as planned. Through original mission records, archival footage, and astronaut recollections, this documentary follows the decisions behind STS-51A, the demanding work outside the shuttle, and the remarkable second lives of Westar 6 and Palapa B2. Why go back for satellites that had already been written off—and what did bringing them home actually prove?

editorialDirection.centralQuestion: Why send astronauts to return two commercially stranded but functioning satellites to Earth, and what made the recovery possible?
editorialDirection.opening: Begin with the authentic For Sale photograph, identify the commercial purpose immediately, then follow the functioning satellites from their failed deployments to the recovery and later return to service.
factualDistinctions: Satellite versus failed PAM-D upper stage
Geostationary target versus unusable low orbit
Additional recovery reimbursement versus total shuttle mission cost
Pre-discussed contingency versus invented spontaneous improvisation
Recovering hardware versus proving that routine commercial shuttle servicing was economical
editorialDirection.sound: Measured curiosity for the orbital problem; restrained forward movement during preparation; greater energy during approach and capture; relief after securing each vehicle; reflective resolution. Keep Charon's authority without a continuous trailer delivery.
editorialDirection.status: Original script and production preparation; final speech durations and audiovisual review remain pending.

scenes.caption: November 1984 · An unusual cargo
scenes.narration:
Two astronauts pose above Discovery's cargo bay with a sign that says For Sale. Below them are two communications satellites, on their way back to Earth. They had already been launched, stranded, and written off by their insurers. Now the hardware was coming home for another chance.

The shuttle crew had gone into orbit to recover commercial property. Their customers wanted to turn insurance losses into machines someone could use again. It would take more than a jetpack and a photograph. One small fitting on a satellite would force the astronauts to change how they worked.

scenes.caption: February 1984 · Challenger
scenes.narration:
The trouble began on a flight that seemed to demonstrate exactly what the shuttle was for. Challenger could carry satellites into low Earth orbit, open its enormous cargo doors, and release them into space. From there, a separate rocket stage would take each satellite much farther out.

On February third, Westar Six left the payload bay. Its destination was a working position high above the equator, serving Western Union's communications network. Western Union had considered other launch options, including Europe's Ariane rocket, before choosing the shuttle on its assessment of price and reliability. Challenger delivered the satellite. Then the upper stage failed to complete its job. Westar was circling Earth, responding to commands, with no way to reach the orbit its customers needed.

A second satellite was still aboard Challenger. Palapa B Two belonged to Indonesia's communications system. Its release was delayed while the first failure was examined. On February sixth, Palapa went out. Its rocket stage also malfunctioned.

Two deployments had produced the same commercial dead end. The failure was in the equipment meant to raise their orbits. The satellites themselves remained healthy. That distinction would eventually make a rescue worth considering. First, it left their owners with an especially frustrating loss: valuable, functioning machines in places where they could not do their intended work.

scenes.caption: The orbit was part of the product
scenes.narration:
For a communications satellite, reaching space is only part of the delivery. At roughly twenty-two thousand three hundred miles above the equator, a satellite can circle Earth in step with the planet's rotation. To a dish on the ground, it stays in the same part of the sky. That is what makes a fixed connection practical.

Westar and Palapa were instead traveling through low, elongated orbits only a few hundred miles above Earth. They swept around the planet rather than remaining over their service areas. Their smaller onboard thrusters could make adjustments. They could not replace the missing climb. The distance between those two orbits was the distance between usable businesses and insurance claims.

scenes.caption: A loss with something left to recover
scenes.narration:
Usually, the paperwork would have outlived the spacecraft. The insurers paid for the losses and acquired salvage rights. A machine stranded in orbit could remain there until its orbit decayed. These machines, however, could still be commanded from the ground. Engineers had something to work with.

If a shuttle could reach them, astronauts might capture them, secure them in the payload bay, and return them for refurbishment. New launches could then put them where the first launches had failed to take them. The insurance settlement had changed who held the financial loss. A recovery might change how much of that loss remained permanent.

scenes.caption: The shuttle's other direction
scenes.narration:
The shuttle carried a possibility that ordinary satellite launches did not: substantial cargo space on the way home. Returning hardware was part of the larger ambition behind the vehicle. Astronauts could deliver, inspect, repair, and retrieve equipment instead of treating every launch as a one-way shipment.

Westar and Palapa offered a concrete test. They were real commercial assets, already built, already launched, and already in trouble. Bringing them back would require a chain of operations no single machine could perform alone. Controllers would prepare their orbits. Pilots would bring Discovery alongside. Spacewalkers would make the capture. Inside the cabin, another astronaut would operate the arm that moved them into the bay.

The financial arrangement depended on a flight that already had other work to do. Discovery would launch two new communications satellites. Recovering the stranded pair would be added to that mission. The initial August agreement covered Palapa alone, with reimbursement of up to four point eight million dollars for recovery expenses. NASA's historical chronology records a payment of five and a half million dollars for bringing both satellites home.

That figure was not the price of an entire shuttle flight. It was the additional recovery payment within a much larger operation. The insurers were buying a chance to recover value from two losses. NASA was combining that chance with an existing mission and a demonstration of what its new vehicle could accomplish.

visualPlan.caption: Anna Fisher at the aft controls

scenes.caption: Rick Hauck · Mission commander
scenes.narration: Commander Rick Hauck was uneasy with the way the recovery was being presented. In his NASA oral history, he recalled objecting to a public announcement that made success sound too straightforward. Even one satellite would be an extraordinary achievement. The insurance participants understood the distinction between property and people. Hauck remembered underwriter Stephen Merrett emphasizing that the crew should not risk its lives merely to bring the hardware back.

visualPlan.caption: The crew with Stephen Merrett · London, 1985

scenes.caption: Five people, one recovery chain
scenes.narration:
Hauck and pilot David Walker would maneuver Discovery and coordinate the work inside. Joe Allen and Dale Gardner would leave the cabin to retrieve the satellites. Anna Fisher would control the Canadian-built robotic arm.

Fisher later described the concentration required while Earth, shuttle, satellite, and arm were moving in her field of view. She was also helping with rendezvous as the spacewalkers prepared. The recovery demanded several jobs at once, with five people dividing the work. Its most famous images would show the men outside. Fisher's positioning of those men and their equipment made much of what followed possible.

scenes.caption: The Manned Maneuvering Unit
scenes.narration:
The jetpack had made its spectacular debut on the same February flight that stranded the satellites. Bruce McCandless flew away from Challenger using the Manned Maneuvering Unit, or M M U. Its nitrogen thrusters allowed an astronaut to translate and turn without a tether connecting him to the shuttle.

That freedom made distant hardware reachable. It also made control essential. The astronaut approaching a satellite had to match its movement closely enough to establish a physical connection. A collision could disturb the target or damage it. The jetpack was a small maneuvering spacecraft wrapped around a person, and the person was about to become part of a much larger moving assembly.

An earlier repair mission had already exposed how difficult that connection could be. In April, astronaut George Nelson tried to attach himself to the Solar Maximum Mission satellite. The capture tool would not engage as expected. The operation disturbed the satellite, and the attempted capture had to be abandoned. Controllers and the shuttle crew eventually stabilized and retrieved Solar Max with the robotic arm, allowing repairs to proceed.

For the next recovery, a successful jetpack flight was only one piece of evidence. The capture interface mattered just as much. A device that worked in preparation still had to meet a real spacecraft, in motion, beyond anyone's ability to walk over and adjust the setup.

visualPlan.caption: George Nelson approaches Solar Max · April 1984

acts.title: The Recovery
acts.subtitle: A practiced plan meets the real spacecraft

scenes.caption: A different way to make contact
scenes.narration:
For Westar and Palapa, engineers developed a long capture device nicknamed the stinger. It would enter the nozzle of the satellite's own apogee motor and lock into place. That motor was separate from the upper stage that had failed months earlier. The astronauts were recovering the satellite, not hauling the failed launch stage back with it.

Once connected, the jetpack could control the satellite's rotation. Fisher could then use the robotic arm to bring the assembly over the bay. A bridge structure fitted above the satellite's antenna would provide another attachment point. The work was divided into steps, each transferring control while keeping the spacecraft secure.

visualPlan.caption: The stinger and an MMU · STS-51A

scenes.caption: Preparing an alternative
scenes.narration: The stinger and bridge were only two of the interfaces they needed. A satellite caught outside still had to become cargo safe to carry through reentry. Engineers prepared the cradles, adapters, and restraints that would make that transformation possible. The spacecraft were already in orbit, beyond any final workshop fit check with the retrieval equipment.

scenes.caption: Making the targets catchable
scenes.narration:
Controllers also had to make the satellites catchable. Before Discovery arrived, they changed the targets' orbits and slowed their rotation. The rendezvous plan had to accommodate two deliveries and two recoveries on a tight propellant budget. NASA's technical history counts forty-four orbital-change maneuvers.

The rescue was already taking shape in commands from the ground. None of that work would appear in the famous For Sale photograph.

scenes.caption: November 8, 1984 · Discovery
scenes.narration:
High-altitude winds delayed the launch by a day. On November eighth, Discovery lifted off with five astronauts, two new satellites, and the equipment for bringing two others home. It was only Discovery's second trip into space.

The crew first had to perform the work that had been scheduled before the recovery was added. Anik D Two would serve Canada. Leasat One would support United States Navy communications. These were deliveries, with their own systems to check and deployments to execute. The bay had to be emptied of its outgoing cargo before it could become a place for the returning spacecraft.

Anik left first. Leasat followed, rolling away from the shuttle in its distinctive spinning release. Both deployments succeeded. The crew could turn its attention to the rendezvous with Palapa.

Hauck and Walker had to place a crewed vehicle beside a target already traveling around Earth. Simply pointing at it and firing the engines would not do. Changes in speed changed the shuttle's orbit, and the crew used a sequence of maneuvers to arrive in the right place at the right time. The recovery plan now depended on bringing two moving vehicles close enough for Allen to cross the remaining distance himself.

scenes.caption: November 12 · Closing on Palapa
scenes.narration:
Discovery approached to within about thirty-five feet of Palapa. Allen and Gardner came through the airlock. Allen fastened himself into the jetpack and took the stinger out toward the satellite. Gardner remained at the payload bay, ready for the next stage of the work.

The gap was small enough to see across and large enough to separate an astronaut from the safety of the vehicle. Allen guided the capture device into the motor opening. Once attached, he used the jetpack's controls to stop the remaining spin. The target and the astronaut could now be handled as a connected system.

From inside Discovery, Fisher moved the arm to a grapple fixture on the capture assembly. Its mechanical hand closed around the attachment point. She could now move Allen and Palapa together over the payload bay.

The first major problem had been solved: the satellite was captured and under control. But it was not ready to come home. Gardner had to fit the bridge structure that would let the arm handle the satellite in the next configuration. The structure would not seat properly. Something on the real spacecraft obstructed the fit.

visualPlan.caption: Preflight bridge design · the attachment that would not seat

scenes.caption: The clearance problem
scenes.narration:
A protruding waveguide fitting interfered with the bridge. It extended farther than the planned clamps could clear. The attachment they had practiced could not be made on the spacecraft in front of them.

The crew had discussed this possibility before launch. Fisher recalled that nobody could check the bridge against the real satellite because it was already in orbit. They had considered a manual alternative with their flight director. Allen now disconnected from the capture assembly and stowed his jetpack. He fixed his feet into a restraint beside the pallet in the bay. The arm released the satellite into his hands.

That transfer changed the work. Allen would keep Palapa steady while Gardner removed the stinger, covered the motor opening, and fitted the adapter needed to secure the satellite in its cradle. Weightlessness made the handling possible. The satellite still had mass, and any push would change its motion.

Allen later said the dramatic picture gave him too much credit. Gardner was doing difficult adapter work largely on his own. One astronaut controlled the machine while the other changed its attachments. Only after they had fitted the landing hardware could they berth and latch Palapa in its cradle. NASA's contemporary mission report called this a practiced backup procedure. The crew had adapted that alternative to the actual problem.

visualPlan.caption: Fisher at the aft station · STS-51A

scenes.caption: One secured
scenes.narration:
After six hours outside, Palapa was secured in its cradle. The first recovery was complete. Between spacewalks, the crew serviced the suits and revised the method for Westar.

Carrying one satellite also complicated the pursuit of the other. Flight director Randy Stone later described the thermal planning involved. The satellite still contained hydrazine, and the team had to consider how the shuttle's orientation would expose it to heat and cold during the next maneuvers. Freezing, damage, or a later leak would create problems for people handling it on the ground. The planning had to protect the spacecraft during the chase and the people who would handle it afterward.

The cargo bay now contained property worth bringing home and hardware that imposed its own conditions on the rest of the flight.

scenes.caption: November 14 · Westar 6
scenes.narration:
For Westar, Gardner flew the jetpack. Allen took the other role. The crew had decided to use the direct handling method and omit the original bridge installation. This time, that choice was part of the revised plan from the start.

Gardner reached the satellite, connected the stinger, and controlled its motion. Gardner guided Westar toward Allen, who was secured to a work platform on the robotic arm. Fisher positioned Allen to receive and hold the satellite while the astronauts prepared it for its cradle. For Palapa, Allen had worked from a fixed restraint beside the pallet. Now the arm itself could position his work platform. The change gave him more freedom to hold the spacecraft where Gardner needed it and reduced the chance of contact with its solar panels.

The second spacewalk lasted five hours and forty-two minutes. Westar joined Palapa in the cargo bay. The mission had now delivered two new satellites and retrieved two others.

At the end of the work, Gardner and Allen posed above the recovered spacecraft with a small sign: For Sale. It was a joke with a real commercial point. The hardware below them had changed from stranded property into cargo that could be inspected, repaired where necessary, and offered another launch.

visualPlan.caption: Westar 6 and Palapa B2 were ready to return

acts.title: A Second Life
acts.subtitle: The recovery only mattered if the hardware could work again

scenes.caption: November 16 · Coming home
scenes.narration:
With both satellites secured, the crew could prepare to come home. The cradles and their restraint systems would hold the satellites through descent and landing. Discovery closed its payload doors and fired its maneuvering engines.

On November sixteenth, Hauck landed at Kennedy Space Center after just under eight days in orbit. Workers on Earth would finally be able to inspect hardware that had been inaccessible since February. The recovery had returned a possibility. Refurbishment and another launch still lay ahead.

scenes.caption: A salvage operation recognized
scenes.narration: At the White House in December, the five astronauts received Lloyd's silver medals for meritorious salvage operations. They visited the insurance market in London the following year. The recognition celebrated a recovery already completed. The commercial result would take considerably longer to arrive.

scenes.caption: 1990 · Westar becomes AsiaSat 1
scenes.narration:
Westar found a new customer in Asia. Hong Kong-based AsiaSat bought it and contracted Hughes to refurbish the spacecraft and adapt its communications payload. On April seventh, nineteen ninety, a Chinese Long March rocket launched it as AsiaSat One.

The recovered satellite entered service the following month. AsiaSat's history records television service in Myanmar and coverage of the Asian Games later that year. A machine originally launched for an American network was helping broadcasters reach audiences in another region. That service was a concrete consequence of bringing usable hardware back, rather than leaving the first failure as its final outcome.

Six days after AsiaSat One launched, a Delta rocket carried the refurbished Palapa into space as Palapa B Two R. It returned to Indonesia's communications system. More than five years separated the rescue from those two new launches. Recovering the machines had preserved an opportunity; turning that opportunity into service had taken additional work, money, and time.

The two functioning spacecraft were now back where their communications equipment could do useful work.

visualPlan.caption: The original Westar 6 hardware · recovered in 1984

scenes.caption: What the mission proved
scenes.narration:
The result demonstrated a capability under particular conditions. The targets were reachable and controllable, and their remaining hardware was worth considering for reuse. A recovery added to a flight with other work cannot tell us what a dedicated commercial rescue flight would have cost.

This became the last mission to use the M M U jetpacks. Satellite servicing continued in other forms. In nineteen ninety-two, another shuttle crew captured a stranded Intelsat satellite, attached a new motor, and released it toward its operating orbit. The ability to intervene survived. Routine return-and-resale remained a much more demanding proposition than a successful spacewalk alone could establish.

scenes.caption: The value of a way back
scenes.narration:
The reason NASA went back begins with two machines that still had useful work ahead of them. Controllers made the targets reachable. Engineers gave the astronauts ways to hold them. Five people carried the recovery through a problem the main procedure could not solve.

Years later, those satellites were carrying signals again. The little For Sale sign above Discovery's cargo bay had pointed toward a real future.

visualPlan.caption: November 1984 · the beginning of a second life
